questions.question: Most crashes happen:

options.text: At speeds greater than 55 mph.
After several hours of riding.
On short trips.
On long trips.

questions.correctAnswerText: On short trips.
questions.explanation: Most motorcycle crashes happen on trips shorter than five miles. They usually occur at speeds slower than 30 mph.

questions.question: When riding a motorcycle, you should:

options.text: Always pick one part of the lane to occupy and never leave that part of the lane.
Vary your lane position as conditions warrant.
Only ride in the center of the lane so other vehicles can see you more easily.
Ride in a zigzag pattern so other drivers notice you.

questions.correctAnswerText: Vary your lane position as conditions warrant.
questions.explanation: No single lane position is always best. Change your position based on road and traffic conditions.

questions.question: To swerve, you should:

options.text: Turn the handlebars quickly.
Shift your weight quickly.
Press the handgrip in the direction of the turn.
Press the handgrip in the opposite direction of the turn.

questions.correctAnswerText: Press the handgrip in the direction of the turn.
questions.explanation: Apply light pressure to the handgrip on the side where you want to go. To swerve left, press the left handgrip, then the right to recover. To swerve right, press the right handgrip, then the left.

questions.question: Riding on the far side of a lane when following another vehicle:

options.text: Is recommended because you will be seen easily.
Is not recommended because drivers seldom use their side mirrors and may not see you.
Is recommended because a passenger in the vehicle may tell the driver that you are there.
Is illegal because you have to ride in the center portion of the lane.

questions.correctAnswerText: Is not recommended because drivers seldom use their side mirrors and may not see you.
questions.explanation: Most drivers check their rearview mirror more often than their side mirrors. Ride in the center of the lane where the driver is most likely to see you in the rearview mirror.

questions.question: When being passed from behind, you should:

options.text: Try to move onto the shoulder.
Use the left portion of your lane.
Use the center portion of your lane.
Use the right portion of your lane.

questions.correctAnswerText: Use the center portion of your lane.
questions.explanation: The center of the lane is safest when being passed. Riding on the side near the passing vehicle risks a collision. Riding on the far side may cause the driver to pull back into your lane too soon.

questions.question: If braking in a curve:

options.text: Only use the front brake.
It will be the same as braking on a straightaway.
You will have more traction as you lean into the curve.
You may have less traction as you lean into the curve.

questions.correctAnswerText: You may have less traction as you lean into the curve.
questions.explanation: You can use both brakes while turning, but be very careful. The tires use some of their grip for turning while leaning, so less grip is available for stopping.

questions.question: When loading cargo onto a motorcycle, you should:

options.text: Pack heavier items in front of the tank bag.
Pack lighter items near the front.
Try to not place items over the rear axle.
Place items behind the rear axle.

questions.correctAnswerText: Pack heavier items in front of the tank bag.
questions.explanation: Put heavier items in front of the tank bag. Load should be over or in front of the rear axle. Placing weight behind the rear axle can hurt your control.

questions.question: What does this sign mean?

options.text: Slow or stop
Left turn
Right turn
Backing up

questions.correctAnswerText: Slow or stop
questions.explanation: A rider can use hand signals instead of or along with turn signals. When the left arm is bent at the elbow and points downward, it means the rider plans to slow down or stop.

questions.question: When riding in a group, inexperienced riders should be placed:

options.text: In the front of the group.
Just behind the lead rider.
At the back of the group.
Anywhere within the group.

questions.correctAnswerText: Just behind the lead rider.
questions.explanation: Inexperienced riders should ride just behind the leader. This way, experienced riders can watch them from behind.

questions.question: Each traffic lane gives the motorcyclist how many paths of travel?

options.text: One
Two
Three
Four

questions.correctAnswerText: Three
questions.explanation: Each traffic lane has three paths for motorcyclists: the left, center, and right portions of the lane.

questions.question: Do you need hearing protection?

options.text: No, a helmet is enough.
Yes, you need it in addition to a helmet.
Only on windy days.
No, not if you carry a passenger.

questions.correctAnswerText: Yes, you need it in addition to a helmet.
questions.explanation: Engine noise and wind noise can damage your hearing, even with a helmet. Hearing protection helps protect your ears while still letting you hear horns and sirens.

questions.question: What is a linked braking system?

options.text: It connects the front and rear brakes so both apply when you use either brake lever.
It connects the front brake to the gear shifter and applies the brake when you downshift.
It connects the rear brake to a foot control.
It connects the rear brake to a handlebar switch.

questions.correctAnswerText: It connects the front and rear brakes so both apply when you use either brake lever.
questions.explanation: A linked braking system connects the front and rear brakes on a motorcycle. When you use either brake lever, both brakes apply. Check your owner's manual for details about your motorcycle's braking system.

questions.question: If you must brake and swerve to avoid a hazard, what should you do?

options.text: Do one action, then the other.
Do both at the same time.
Always brake first, then swerve.
Only use the brakes.

questions.correctAnswerText: Do one action, then the other.
questions.explanation: Brake and swerve separately, not at the same time. You can brake then swerve, or swerve then brake.

questions.question: The center of a lane often has an oily strip. Is this area safe for motorcyclists?

options.text: Never safe.
Usually safe, unless the road is wet.
Usually safe, unless it is sunny.
Always safe, no matter the weather.

questions.correctAnswerText: Usually safe, unless the road is wet.
questions.explanation: Oil drippings from cars collect in the center of traffic lanes. When the road is dry, this area usually has enough traction for motorcycles. When the road is wet, the oil makes it slippery. The oily strip is usually narrow, so you can often ride to one side and still be in the center portion of the lane.

questions.question: If your front wheel begins to skid, what should you do?

options.text: Keep the front brake engaged and ride out the skid.
Keep the front brake engaged and release the rear brake.
Release the front brake immediately, then re-engage it.
Release the front brake and increase pressure on the rear brake.

questions.correctAnswerText: Release the front brake immediately, then re-engage it.
questions.explanation: If your front wheel locks while braking, release the front brake completely right away. Then apply it again smoothly.

questions.question: To carry a passenger, you may need to adjust all of the following, except:

options.text: Tire pressure.
Mirror positions.
Headlight position.
Brake light position.

questions.correctAnswerText: Brake light position.
questions.explanation: A passenger's weight changes how your motorcycle sits. You may need to adjust tire pressure, suspension, shocks, headlight, and mirrors. You do not need to adjust the brake light position.

questions.question: When planning a long group ride, which idea should you NOT use?

options.text: Plan travel distances based on the least experienced rider.
Skip breaks to reach the destination faster.
Put inexperienced riders behind the leaders.
Ride in a staggered formation.

questions.correctAnswerText: Skip breaks to reach the destination faster.
questions.explanation: Plan routes based on the least experienced rider's skill level. Take regular breaks to reduce fatigue. Put inexperienced riders behind leaders so experienced riders can watch them. Ride in a staggered formation for safety.

questions.question: A small animal enters your lane while you are in traffic. What should you do?

options.text: Swerve into other lanes to avoid hitting the animal.
Switch lanes as quickly as possible.
Stay in your lane.
Flash your lights to scare the animal.

questions.correctAnswerText: Stay in your lane.
questions.explanation: Avoid hitting animals when you can do so safely. In traffic, stay in your lane. Swerving into another lane risks hitting another vehicle. Hitting a small animal is safer than hitting a vehicle.

questions.question: Another vehicle is passing you on your left. What should you do?

options.text: Move as far to the right as possible.
Move to the shoulder.
Ride in the center portion of your lane.
Ride in the left portion of your lane.

questions.correctAnswerText: Ride in the center portion of your lane.
questions.explanation: When being passed, ride in the center portion of your lane. Moving toward the passing vehicle increases collision risk. Moving away may cause them to merge back too soon. Stay centered in your lane.

questions.question: When it is raining, where is it usually best to ride?

options.text: In the center of the lane.
On the side of the road until the rain stops.
In the tire tracks left by cars.
At a faster speed.

questions.correctAnswerText: In the tire tracks left by cars.
questions.explanation: Wet pavement is very slippery when rain first starts. Oil from cars has not washed away yet. Ride in the tire tracks left by cars. The left tire track is often the best choice, though this may vary.

questions.question: If you need to swerve, what should you do?

options.text: Shift your weight quickly.
Turn your handlebars quickly.
Press the handgrip in the direction you want to turn.
Press the handgrip in the opposite direction of the turn.

questions.correctAnswerText: Press the handgrip in the direction you want to turn.
questions.explanation: To swerve safely, press the handgrip toward the direction you want to go. To swerve left, press the left handgrip. To swerve right, press the right handgrip. Then press the opposite handgrip to straighten out.

questions.question: What does this sign mean?

options.text: Speed up.
Slow down.
Ride in a single line.
The group will exit at the next ramp.

questions.correctAnswerText: Ride in a single line.
questions.explanation: When the lead rider raises their left arm and points with one finger, it means all riders should form a single-file line. This is an important hand signal used when riding in groups.

questions.question: When should a passenger get on a motorcycle?

options.text: Before the engine starts.
After the engine starts.
As far back on the seat as possible.
While holding onto the seat.

questions.correctAnswerText: After the engine starts.
questions.explanation: Passengers should board only after the engine is running and in neutral. They should sit as far forward as they can without blocking the driver's control. Passengers should hold onto the driver's waist, hips, or belt.

questions.question: What helps you ride safely on slippery roads?

options.text: Using only the front brake.
Using both brakes.
Using the center lane.
Keeping your normal speed or speeding up.

questions.correctAnswerText: Using both brakes.
questions.explanation: On slippery roads, slow down and use both brakes gently. Avoid quick movements. Stay away from the center lane and follow the tire tracks left by cars. Watch for hazards like oil spots and loose gravel.

questions.question: Which statement is true about motorcycle brakes?

options.text: The front and rear brakes are equally powerful.
The front brake is more powerful than the rear brake.
The rear brake is more powerful than the front brake.
Only use the front brake when stopping.

questions.correctAnswerText: The front brake is more powerful than the rear brake.
questions.explanation: The front brake provides most of the stopping power—at least 70 percent. Always use both brakes when you slow down or stop.
